content: Tier 4 is the machinery: the endings and
the sound shifts that give a Norman word
away.
-tion and -sion make a noun out of a
verb. They name the act, or what the act
leaves behind.
motion      beside swing
vision      beside sight
question    beside asking
solution    beside answer
The ending is Latin and it reached us
through French. Once you have it you
will see it on every page you read.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: nouns in -tion and -sion.
-age makes a noun from a verb or from a
thing: the act, the result, or the whole
collection of something.
damage      beside harm
luggage     beside bags
message     beside word
foliage     beside leaves
English liked the ending enough to hang
it on words of its own. Luggage is the
Norse lug under a French suffix, and
wreckage is the Norse wreck.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: nouns in -age.
-ment turns a verb into a noun as well,
but it names the thing done rather than
the doing: not judging but a judgment.
achievement beside deed
agreement   beside deal
judgment    beside doom
equipment   beside gear
Doom is the Old English dom, a ruling
handed down in court. The Norman word
took the courtroom and left doom the
dark end of the meaning.
THE NEXT 24 CARDS: nouns in -ment.
The Normans spoke the northern French
of Rouen, not the French of Paris. The
two said the same words differently,
and English took both.
warranty    beside guarantee
ward        beside guard
wile        beside guile
war         beside guerrilla
Norman kept the Frankish w. Paris
turned it into gu. English ended up
with both halves of its own conquest
and found work for each.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: the w and the gu,
and a few ca words beside them.
The same split, on another sound. Where
Rouen said ca, Paris said cha, and
English has the pairs to prove it.
castle      the Paris form is chateau
cattle      beside chattel
chase       beside catch
chieftain   beside captain
Cattle and chattel are one Latin word,
capitale, property: one went to the
farm, one stayed in the law. Regal and
royal are one word too, one taken
straight and one worn down in French.
THE NEXT 13 CARDS: the ca and the cha.
Three endings, all of them French, each
of them turning a word into an
adjective: -ous, full of; -ive, tending
to; -al, belonging to.
precious    beside dear
famous      beside well-known
active      beside busy
final       beside last
The plain twin is nearly always one
short word: dear, busy, last. The
French one carries its ending with it,
and you can hear it coming.
THE NEXT 25 CARDS: adjectives in -ous,
-ive and -al.
-ance and -ence name a quality or a
state. They are one Latin ending in two
forms, -antia and -entia, split by the
vowel of the Latin verb beneath.
abundance   beside wealth
distance    beside span
absence     beside lack
confidence  beside trust
English had its own way of doing this
with -ness and -hood. It kept those and
took the French pair as well.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: nouns in -ance and
-ence.
The same ending, twenty more words. By
now the shape should arrive before the
meaning does.
existence   beside being
patience    beside forbearance
vengeance   beside getting even
diligence   beside hard work
Look at the right column. English says
these things too, but it says them in
two or three short words, and French
says them in one long one. That is one
of the plainest marks of the two layers.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: the rest of the
-ance and -ence nouns.
